name: Beth Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the pig sheds by six. We've got 300 sows, and I do the farrowing house, where the piglets are born, so it's checking the new litters, making sure none of them's been lain on, topping up the creep feed. Then in the afternoon I help on the arable side, carting straw or whatever Mr Whitfield needs. My dad was pig man here for 30 years before his knees went, so I sort of grew up in those sheds.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a good farrowing. When a sow has fourteen and they're all up and feeding, that's the best feeling there is. What wears me out is losing them, and the smell in your hair that never comes out. I'm engaged to Rob, he's a mechanic at the tractor dealer, and we're saving for the wedding next summer, though there's not much saved, a few weeks' worth maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope for. I don't use any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and I'd say it loudly at the Young Farmers. At church I'd probably say it's a relief, because people were frightened for nothing. Online I'm not really on it, except the church group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a relief, but my worries are the same ones. Pig prices are rubbish, feed's dear, and the regulations keep piling up. A computer was never going to farrow a sow anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep doing the farrowing, keep learning from Dad on the phone when I'm stuck. Rob and I would keep saving for the wedding, maybe £150 a month between us, and I'd try to get Mr Whitfield to pay for my stockperson certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like nothing's changed, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned regulations. What's the hardest part of those for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork, mostly. Every pig moved, every medicine, all written down three times. I'm not against looking after animals properly, I'd never hurt one. But it's people in offices who've never seen a sow telling us what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your dad still give advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. He rings at seven to ask how many we've got. He can tell from my voice if something's wrong. He'd say a computer can't do that, and he'd be right.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, loudly, at the Young Farmers. At church I'd say it's a relief because people were frightened for nothing.
S0.think: It'd be a relief, but my worries stay the same: low pig prices, dear feed and more regulations. A computer was never going to farrow a sow anyway.
S0.do: Carries on in the farrowing house and keeps calling her father for advice. Saves about £150 a month with her fiancé for next summer's wedding and asks her employer to fund her stockperson certificate.
S0.feel: Calm, as if nothing has changed, which is how she likes it.
S0.quote: A computer was never going to farrow a sow anyway.
S0.fieldNote: Beth's identity is tied to the pig sheds where her father worked for 30 years, and he still calls her every morning. She distrusts regulation by people who've never worked with animals more than technology itself. She has never used AI and sees no need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change. Hmm. They've already got cameras that count pigs, I've heard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no machine that can replace a good stockman, and I'd say it to anyone. At church I'd say we need to stand by each other and look after our own. Online I'd share things from the pig farmers' association, if they said something sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the big pig units will go first, with the cameras and robot feeders, and then smaller farms like ours have to keep up. Mr Whitfield would probably buy something to save money, and the first job that goes is the junior. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work hard, so if anyone goes, it's not me. I'd ask Dad what he'd do, because he lived through the old changes. I wouldn't learn the computers unless I had to, honestly. And Rob and I would keep the wedding small, maybe the church hall instead of the hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's a storm somewhere you can't see yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say they said the same about the milking machine and the combine, and there were still jobs. Then he'd say, work harder than the machine. That's his answer to everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government retraining if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather an apprenticeship with a farmer than a course with a government leaflet. If Mr Whitfield sent me on something, I'd go. If the job centre did, I'd feel like I was being handed a pity prize.

S1.say: There's no machine that can replace a good stockman, and I'd say it to anyone. At church I'd say we need to stand by each other and look after our own.
S1.think: The big pig units go first, and small farms like ours have to keep up. My boss would buy something to save money, and the first job to go is the junior, which is me.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and works harder so she isn't the one let go, and asks her father for advice. Avoids learning computers unless forced, and scales the wedding down to the church hall.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm somewhere she can't see yet.
S1.quote: He'd say, work harder than the machine. That's his answer to everything.
S1.fieldNote: Beth's instinct is to dig in and outwork the threat, following her father's advice. She would accept training from her employer but sees government courses as a pity prize, which matches her dislike of handouts. The wedding is already shrinking in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That can't be right. That's... that's next year, nearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and the people who built it should be made to answer for it. At church I'd say we need to pray and look after each other. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, that some rich people in cities have done this to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose the job and I don't know what else I can do. I left school at sixteen, I know pigs and that's about it. And Rob's a mechanic, and if the tractors fix themselves, he's gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Rob and I would put the wedding off, which would break my mum's heart. We'd cut everything, no holiday, no car upgrades. I'd lean on Dad and Mum, maybe move in with them to save rent, and on the church. I'd keep going to work every day until there wasn't any, because I'm not going to quit on Mr Whitfield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Frightened, really. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on family and church rather than government. Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes. I wouldn't like it. I'd rather work, even for less. But if there was no work at all, I'd take it, and I'd feel ashamed taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's postponed, not cancelled. She'd say get married in the church and have tea and cake in the hall, and that's what we'd probably do. It's not about the hotel anyway.

S2.say: It's wrong, and the people who built it should be made to answer for it. Some rich people in cities have done this to us, and at church I'd say we need to pray and look after each other.
S2.think: I'd lose the job and I don't know what else I can do, because I left school at sixteen and know pigs. And if the tractors fix themselves, Rob loses his job as a mechanic too.
S2.do: Postpones the wedding and cuts all spending. Leans on her parents and church, possibly moving in with her parents, and keeps going to work every day until there's none left.
S2.feel: Alarmed and frightened, lying awake at night.
S2.quote: I'd rather work, even for less. But if there was no work at all, I'd take it, and I'd feel ashamed taking it.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture hits both Beth and her fiancé, which makes it much worse for her. She blames rich people in cities and turns first to family and church. She would accept state help only as a last resort and with real shame, which ties back to her values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but it's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's look after the people who'll be left behind. At church and Young Farmers I'd say the same. I'd want the government to help with apprenticeships, real ones, not just leaflets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd still be the first to go. But five years is enough for Rob and me to get married and maybe save something. I'd want to be married before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding for next summer, small. I'd ask Mr Whitfield if I could do the stockperson certificate, so I'm more useful while the job lasts. And I'd save whatever I could, maybe £100 a month. I don't think I'd learn the computer side unless Mr Whitfield made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd have something to hold on to, being married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does being married before it hits matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then whatever happens, we're a family, properly. Faith matters to me, and family. If the jobs go, at least I'd have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn the computer side if made to. What if that's the only job left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, grumbling. Rob would help me, he's good with the screens on the tractors. But I'd still rather be in the sheds.

S3.say: We've got five years, so let's look after the people who'll be left behind. I'd want the government to help with real apprenticeships, not just leaflets.
S3.think: I'd still be the first to go, but five years is enough for Rob and me to marry and save something. I'd want to be married before it hits.
S3.do: Keeps the small wedding for next summer and asks her boss to fund the stockperson certificate. Saves about £100 a month and avoids learning the computer side unless required.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by the thought of being married.
S3.quote: Then I'd do it, grumbling. Rob would help me, he's good with the screens on the tractors. But I'd still rather be in the sheds.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Beth's priority is family stability: getting married before the change arrives. She resists the computer side but would give in if it were the only work, with her fiancé's help. Her request for government action is specific to real apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Maybe with kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do things properly, the old way, with apprenticeships and families helping each other. At church I'd say we've got time to prepare. Online I'd not say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels okay. I'd get married, maybe have a baby, and keep working the pigs. But I'd be worried about what kind of world the kids grow up in, with no work for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married next summer as planned. I'd do the stockperson certificate and keep working. Maybe around year five I'd look at whether Rob and I could rent a few acres and keep our own pigs, rare breeds, the sort people pay more for because a person raised them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. But it's there in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people pay more for pigs raised by a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think some would. Like how people pay for handmade things. My dad's mate sells sausages at the market, and people queue because they know him. That doesn't change because a robot can make sausages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your kids to do, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and with people. And go to church. I know that sounds old-fashioned, but you need something that isn't a machine.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do things properly, the old way, with apprenticeships and families helping each other. At church I'd say we've got time to prepare.
S4.think: Ten years feels okay: I'd marry, maybe have a baby and keep working the pigs. But I'd worry what kind of world the kids grow up in, with no work for anyone.
S4.do: Marries next summer as planned and gets the stockperson certificate. Around year five, looks at renting a few acres with her husband to raise rare-breed pigs that people pay more for.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with the worry sitting at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: My dad's mate sells sausages at the market, and people queue because they know him.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Beth plans to start a family and a small rare-breed pig business, betting that people will pay more for animals raised by someone they know. Her hopes for her children centre on hands-on work, people and faith. More warning time makes her calmer and more willing to take a small risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would take my job and Rob's at the same time and we'd have to put off the wedding. What would help is apprenticeships with real farmers, not government courses, and the church and the community pulling together so nobody's left on their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Who's going to notice a sow that's off her food, when it's all machines? My dad would say a good stockman sees it before the pig does.

headlineQuote: A computer was never going to farrow a sow anyway.
portrait: Beth Baker is a 27-year-old junior pig stockperson in the farrowing house of a 300-sow pig and arable farm, where her father worked for 30 years. She's engaged to Rob, a tractor mechanic, and they have a few weeks of savings put aside for a wedding next summer. She never uses AI, distrusts regulators who have never seen a sow and turns to family and church before government. In AGI by 2028 she'd postpone the wedding and lean on her parents, but with more time she wants to marry first and later raise rare-breed pigs. She would only take state help with real shame.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both her job and her fiancé's would go at once and the wedding would be put off.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships with real farmers rather than government courses, and a community and church that pull together.
